hero.title:
I'm Unemployed.
So I Hired an AI
to Get Me Hired.

items.text: [X] job applications. Zero hours of my time.
I built a system that finds jobs, rewrites my resume for each one, and applies — while I sleep.
I haven't opened LinkedIn in a week.

musicCue.title: Suspended Pulse
musicCue.desc: Atmospheric drone, quiet anticipation. Single repeating note that lets your VO sit on top.
musicCue.note: Holds through Frame. Don't compete with the cold open.

shotList.desc: Dashboard scrolling, applications auto-filling. No face yet.
Counter ticking up to [X] applications. Number visible on screen.
Cut to your face for "I haven't opened LinkedIn in a week." Small smile.

items.text: I built this in a weekend with Claude Code — and I mean Claude actually designed the architecture, not just wrote the code.
By the end of this video you'll see exactly how it finds jobs, tailors my resume to each one, applies, and fixes itself when it breaks.
And after watching, you'll probably want to build one too.

musicCue.title: (carries over)
musicCue.desc: No transition. Music carries from the cold open into the contract.
musicCue.note: Light build cued for the pivot into Tension.

shotList.desc: Direct camera. Slightly tighter framing than the rest of the video.
4-flash montage previewing each beat: find / tailor / apply / heal. ~2s each.
Back to face for the "build one too" close. Subtle smirk.

items.text: Here's the thing though.
When you see a build like this, you probably assume the impressive part is the AI — the so-called "intelligence" picking jobs and rewriting the resume.
That's wrong.
The LLM is the easy part. OpenRouter plus a prompt does the resume tailoring in twenty lines of code. Anyone watching this could ship that on a Saturday.
The hard part — the part that makes this an actual system instead of a demo — is what happens at 3 AM when LinkedIn changes a button and your script silently breaks for a week before you notice.
That's the part nobody builds. That's why every "AI agent" you've seen on Twitter looks magical for 90 seconds and then dies the second it touches a real website.
The intelligence isn't the moat. The loop is.

musicCue.title: Forward Pulse
musicCue.desc: Confident forward push. Underlines the contrarian thesis without overpowering it.
musicCue.note: Lift on "That's wrong." Drop slightly under "The intelligence isn't the moat."

items.text: First problem — finding jobs is the worst part of being unemployed.
While I was making coffee this morning, it had already pulled the day's listings from LinkedIn — exactly the kind of role I'd search for myself. Then it did the same thing on Indeed.
Greenhouse is next. Each platform I add is one more module hitting the same queue. It compounds.

musicCue.title: Working
musicCue.desc: Forward motion, system-at-work feel. New track signals the build phase.
musicCue.note: Hard cut on Beat 1 opening. Hold through Beat 2.

shotList.desc: "First problem — finding jobs is the worst part of being unemployed."

Browser scraping LinkedIn listings — automation visible.

Lower-third: GREENHOUSE NEXT

animation.brief: Promise Row 02 animation. Same structure as Row 01. File: Promise Row 02 - Tailors.mp4 (done)

items.text: A tailored resume makes you 6 times more likely to land an interview. That's not a tip — that's from 3.2 million applications.
Here's where most people stop. They paste the job description into ChatGPT, get a tailored resume back, copy it over. Fine for one job. But you can't do that 50 times a day.

So I had Claude wire up the rewrite. Take this listing — they wanted distributed systems experience. The model found the bullet on my resume that matched, pulled it to the top, and rewrote it in the exact language they used.
Same resume going in, hundreds of versions coming out, one for each job.

musicCue.title: (continues)
musicCue.desc: Energy lifts under the resume tailoring example.

shotList.desc: "A tailored resume makes you 6 times more likely..."
Big stat overlay: 6× MORE LIKELY · 3.2M APPLICATIONS
ChatGPT used manually — paste JD, get resume, copy. Show how slow it is.
Side-by-side: original resume vs. tailored. Distributed-systems bullet highlighted.
"Same resume going in, hundreds of versions coming out, one for each job."

animation.brief: Promise Row 03 animation. Same structure as Row 01. File: Promise Row 03 - Applies.mp4 (done)

items.text: Now the part that actually saves time.

Watch this. It opens the application page, walks through the form, hits submit — about twelve seconds, start to finish. The confirmation page screenshots to a log with a timestamp, so I can prove it actually went through.
That log matters in a second.

musicCue.title: Climbing
musicCue.desc: Watch-this energy. Tension climbs into the submission moment.
musicCue.note: Lift right before "twelve seconds, start to finish."

shotList.desc: "Now the part that actually saves time."
Watch-this sequence: bot opens application page, fills form, submits.
Stopwatch animation hitting 12s.
Confirmation screenshot saving to log. Timestamp visible.

animation.brief: Promise Row 04 animation. Same structure as Row 01. File: Promise Row 04 - Fixes.mp4 (done)

items.text: Here's the part that broke my brain.
And this is the part nobody builds.
So I gave Claude Code access to the logs.
This happened on day three. LinkedIn changed a button selector. The applier crashed.
The log caught it. Claude Code read it, figured out what broke, and fixed the function. The next application went through.
No human in the loop. I was asleep.
I went to sleep with broken code. Woke up with working code. Nobody touched it.

musicCue.title: DROP — Suspended
musicCue.desc: Strip everything back. The reveal needs space — your face, the screen, the words.
musicCue.note: Music swells back in on "Woke up with working code." That's the catharsis.

shotList.desc: "Here's the part that broke my brain." Lean in slightly.
Black card / pause for tonal shift. ~1s of held black.
Log file showing the day-three crash entry. Red error highlighted.
Claude Code reading log, diagnosing, patching the function.
Next successful application going through.
"I went to sleep with broken code. Woke up with working code." Slow delivery. Hold on face.

animation.brief: Dashboard title card. Large italic 'The dashboard' at 200px rises in. Eyebrow label 'UI' and flanking lines appear first. Accent underline sweeps in last. File: the-dashboard.mp4 (done)

items.text: Last piece. I needed to actually see what this thing was doing.
Every job it applies to gets a card. Title, company, link to the listing, the resume version it sent, screenshots of every step. All timestamped.
And then the part I actually look at every morning.

A heatmap. Same idea as the GitHub contribution graph, but for applications. Dark green squares are heavy days. Light squares are light days. Empty squares mean something broke — and I check the logs to see why.
I don't read the dashboard to manage the system. I read it to trust the system.
Because if you're going to let an AI run your job search, you need to be able to see exactly what it did when you weren't looking.

musicCue.title: Reflective
musicCue.desc: Settled, trust. The system is real and it's yours. Quieter than Beats 1–3.

shotList.desc: "Last piece. I needed to actually see what this thing was doing."
Dashboard card view — scrolling through applications.
Heatmap visualization. Your morning glance.
"I read it to trust the system." Hit "trust" hard.

items.text: So — did it work?
[X] applications submitted. [Y] hours of my time. The system has been running for [Z] days and I haven't touched it.
But honestly — that's not the part of this that matters.

musicCue.title: (continues)
musicCue.desc: Hold under the receipts. Don't change tracks for the close.
musicCue.note: Soft hold through "that's not the part of this that matters."

shotList.desc: Direct camera. "So — did it work?"
Big numbers reveal: [X] applications · [Y] hours · [Z] days
"But honestly — that's not the part of this that matters."

items.text: Most AI agents fail because nobody builds the loop around them. The model isn't the bottleneck.
AI stopped being a tool the day it started fixing its own bugs.

musicCue.title: DROP — Crystal
musicCue.desc: Music drops out under the crystallize line. The line lands in air.
musicCue.note: One full beat of silence after "fixing its own bugs." Then resolution swells in.

shotList.desc: Slow push-in or hold. No cuts.
Crystallize line as on-screen text: AI stopped being a tool the day it started fixing its own bugs.

items.text: If you can write code, open Claude Code tonight.
Build the dumbest version of this you can — one job board, no resume tailoring, nothing fancy.
But build the loop. Make it log everything. Make it catch its own errors. Make it heal itself when something breaks. That's the part you have to feel work to understand.
The people who build these systems are going to be fine. Be one of them.

musicCue.title: Resolution
musicCue.desc: Slight rise into the call to action. Not triumphant — settled.
musicCue.note: Tail out under "Be one of them." Let it ring for a half-second after VO ends.

shotList.desc: Direct address.
Hands at keyboard. Claude Code opening in terminal.
"Be one of them." Hold for a beat. Cut.

rollout.label: Posting Cadence
rollout.title: Stagger across ~3 weeks. Don't dump.
rollout.sub: Strongest first. Different hook angles spaced apart. Bank the medium ones for slow weeks.

days.what: Long-form video launches. Same day, post Short 01 · self-healing. Most visceral payoff. Doubles as a teaser — viewers who want context click through to the full build.
Short 02 · the 6× stat. Different audience hook (career-anxious vs. AI-curious), so the algorithm reads it as fresh terrain instead of a sequel.

Short 03 for the next "AI agent went viral" moment on the timeline — ride the topic. Short 04 for whenever the dashboard heatmap gets re-photographed cleanly. No fixed dates — these are slow-week ammo.

If Short 01 underperforms in 48 hours, do not follow with Short 03. Both lean on the same thesis — back-to-back failures will train the algorithm against the topic. Pivot to Short 02 instead and let the channel cool.

rollout.label: Rollout Plan
rollout.title: Spread across ~7 days. Don't dump.
rollout.sub: Native video first for reach. Thread later for depth. Receipts and quote pace the cycle.

days.what: YouTube video goes live. Same day, post the native video clip (Post 02). Highest-reach format on X — let the algorithm warm to the topic before you start telling people what it means.
Receipts tweet (Post 03). Dashboard heatmap. The audience that saw yesterday's clip now sees the proof — curiosity gap → click. Different hook, same audience, second touch.

The thread (Post 01). By now the receipts and clip are circulating. The thread expands the contrarian thesis for the people asking "okay but how though?" Quote-RT the original video clip in the thread for context.
Image quote (Post 04). Caps the cycle. Surfaces the crystallize line for everyone who missed the earlier posts. Low-effort, high-quotability — and by now the audience has earned the line.
If video clip + thread underperform in the first 48 hours, skip Post 04 entirely. Don't run the medium-strength post into a cold audience.

summary.label: Assessment
summary.inv: Personal stake: present and visible — unemployment is the setup, building the system is the response. Macro insight: strong — "the loop, not the model" is the kind of operational take that career-adjacent professionals recognize and share. Visual evidence for native video: insufficient for LinkedIn. The self-healing clip works on Twitter and Shorts because those audiences are already technical-curious. On LinkedIn, a 75s screen recording of Claude Code patching a function needs more setup than the format allows — it reads like a product demo, not a human story. Skip native video here. Crossover appeal: high. Job seekers, engineering managers, recruiters, and people generally anxious about AI in the workplace all have a stake in this post. That's the rare kind of crossover that earns distribution on LinkedIn.

posts.headline: I'm unemployed. So I built an AI that applies to jobs while I sleep.

specs.label: Full post text
paragraphs: I'm unemployed. So I built an AI that applies to jobs while I sleep.
Not a script that fills out a form. A system — one that finds jobs, rewrites my resume to match each one, submits, and fixes itself when it breaks.
[X] applications submitted. [Y] hours of my time.
Here's what I actually learned building it.
The model is the easy part.

Tailored resumes make you 6x more likely to land an interview — that stat is from 3.2 million applications. Wiring up an LLM to do the rewriting took me about 20 lines of code. Anyone reading this could ship that on a Saturday afternoon.
The hard part is what happens at 3 AM when LinkedIn changes a button and your script silently breaks for a week before you notice.
Every "AI agent" I've seen fails here. The demo looks clean for 90 seconds. Then it touches a real website, gets a DOM change it didn't expect, and dies quietly.
So I built the loop around the model instead.

Every step logs to a file. Every failure surfaces to a queue that Claude Code reads, diagnoses, and patches before the next run. Day three of running it, LinkedIn moved a button selector. The system caught it, rewrote the failing function, and the next application went through.

That's the shift I didn't expect: I stopped managing the system and started trusting it. The dashboard I built isn't about oversight — it's about confidence. A heatmap of every application, every timestamp, every screenshot of the confirmation page. Not so I can micromanage it. So I know it's running when I'm not watching.
The intelligence isn't the moat. The loop is.
If you're in a job search right now — or you manage people who are — the leverage isn't applying more. It's building the system that applies for you, and trusting it enough to sleep.

whyFormat.label: Why written post, not native video
whyFormat.text: The self-healing moment is the most cinematic beat in this script — but LinkedIn's native video audience skews toward polished talking-head content, not screen recordings. A 75s clip of Claude Code patching a function loses the human stakes entirely. The written post leads with unemployment (personal), builds to operational insight (professional), and lands on a line that managers and job seekers can share with their own audience. That's the LinkedIn flywheel: personal story + transferable lesson = reach beyond your followers.

rollout.label: Posting Notes
rollout.title: Post same day the video goes live.
rollout.sub: LinkedIn and YouTube serve different audiences — post them together, not sequentially.

days.what: YouTube video launches. Post the LinkedIn written post the same day — ideally within 2 hours of the video going live. The audiences don't overlap much; this isn't cannibalism, it's parallel distribution.

Drop the YouTube link immediately as the first comment. Do it before the post gets any engagement — don't wait. LinkedIn suppresses external links in the body; the comment placement is the workaround, and it's standard practice now.
Don't edit the post body after it starts getting traction. LinkedIn's algorithm treats edits as resets. If the numbers are moving, leave it alone.

The comments that ask "how did you build this?" are the signal. Reply with one sentence and the YouTube link. Don't paste the full build in the thread — that kills the click-through. Curiosity gap stays open until they watch.
